newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate clears Albright as secretary of state.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate clears Albright as secretary of state.

text.p: The Senate on Wednesday voted unanimously to confirm Madeleine Albright as America's first woman secretary of state and the first Cabinet officer to be approved for President Bill Clinton's second term.

The Senate then moved to debate and vote on confirmation of former Senator William Cohen as defence secretary - the only Republican named to Democrat Clinton's Cabinet and the second member of a national security team that also includes former national security adviser Anthony lake as CIA director.
Albright was confirmed by a 99-0 vote.
A similar unanimous approval was expected for Cohen, the former Maine legislator who has just retired from the Senate after 18 years and has many friends there in both parties.

Albright, 59, has been serving as Clinton's ambassador to the United Nations where her stand against reappointment of Boutros Boutros-Ghali as secretary general won her points with Republican critics of the world body.

Boutros-Ghali's successor was arriving in Washington on Wednesday for talks with administration officials and members of Congress on U.N. reforms and payment of the $1.3 billion U.S. debt to the world body.

Albright succeeds Warren Christopher as secretary of state to become the premier voice in U.S. foreign policy. Known for forthright speech and avoidance of diplomatic circumlocution, she was warmly praised by members of both parties.

Born in Prague, she says her political life was moulded by the diplomatic appeasement of Adolf Hitler at Munich and by the experience of bomb shelters in London where her family fled the Nazi invasion.

The evident high regard in which she is held among members of Congress may well be crucial as she lobbies hard for more funding for the foreign affairs budget, which Christopher has complained has been cut to dangerous levels.
At the U.S. mission to the U.N. in New York, Albright told reporters the Senate vote "signals a new era of bipartisan foreign policy and I can't wait to get started."

Senator Jesse Helms, a North Carolina Republican and chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, supported Albright's nomination but faulted Clinton's foreign policy over the past four years. He said it had given "a message of weakened resolve around the world."

Speaking during a debate on the confirmation, Helms said that "we'll be watching her closely" to see if Albright had learned from the past "disasters," including U.S. involvement in Somalia and Haiti.
Helms also said he would reintroduce a plan to reorganize the State Department, saying it would save $1 billion a year.
Last year the Clinton administration and Helms were deadlocked for months over his plan to eliminate three foreign policy agencies. Clinton eventually killed the bill by veto.
Albright, in her testimony to the Foreign Relations Committee, said she had an open mind about the proposal.

Judd Gregg, a Republican senator from New Hampshire, voiced concern that the Clinton administration would seek funds to pay U.S. arrears to the U.N. He said there had been much talk but little success on reform and "suspect" budget cuts.
